```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5
)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

# Introduction

This code-through explains how to explore and change a dataset in R. I use the
`iris` dataset because it is already included in R, so no file needs to be
downloaded. The dataset contains measurements for 150 flowers from three iris
species: setosa, versicolor, and virginica.

By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to:

- view a dataset;
- select and filter observations;
- create a new variable;
- summarize information by group; and
- create a graph with `ggplot2`.

# Load and Preview the Data

First, I copy the built-in dataset into an object called `flowers`. The
`head()` function prints the first six rows. This is a quick way to understand
what the data looks like.

```{r load-data}
flowers <- iris
head(flowers)
```

Each row represents one flower. The first four columns contain measurements in
centimeters, and `Species` gives the flower's species.

# Check the Dataset Structure

The `glimpse()` function shows the number of rows and columns, the type of each
variable, and a few values. The `count()` function shows how many flowers belong
to each species.

```{r inspect-data}
glimpse(flowers)

flowers %>%
  count(Species)
```

The dataset has 150 rows and 5 columns. It has 50 flowers from each species, so
the three groups are the same size.

# Select and Filter Rows

Sometimes we only need a small part of a dataset. In the next step, I use
`filter()` to keep only setosa flowers. I use `select()` to keep three useful
columns, and `slice_head()` to print only the first six rows.

```{r filter-data}
setosa_sample <- flowers %>%
  filter(Species == "setosa") %>%
  select(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length, Species) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6)

setosa_sample
```

The new object is smaller than the original dataset. It contains only setosa
flowers and only the columns selected in the code.

# Create a New Variable

The `mutate()` function creates or changes a variable. Here, I create
`Petal.Ratio` by dividing petal length by petal width. The `round()` function
makes the result easier to read.

```{r mutate-data}
flowers_changed <- flowers %>%
  mutate(Petal.Ratio = round(Petal.Length / Petal.Width, 2))

flowers_changed %>%
  select(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, Petal.Ratio, Species) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

The original dataset had five columns. The changed dataset has a sixth column,
`Petal.Ratio`, while the original measurements remain unchanged.

# Summarize the Species

The `group_by()` and `summarise()` functions work together. First, the flowers
are placed into species groups. Then R calculates the number of flowers and the
average sepal and petal lengths for every group.

```{r summary-table}
species_summary <- flowers %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(
    Number_of_Flowers = n(),
    Average_Sepal_Length = round(mean(Sepal.Length), 2),
    Average_Petal_Length = round(mean(Petal.Length), 2)
  )

kable(
  species_summary,
  caption = "Average Flower Measurements by Species",
  align = "c"
)
```

The table shows that setosa has the shortest average petals, while virginica
has the longest average petals.

# Make a Graph

A graph can make group differences easier to see. The following scatterplot
compares sepal length with petal length. Color represents species, and
`geom_smooth()` adds one trend line for each group.

```{r scatterplot, fig.cap="Sepal Length and Petal Length by Iris Species"}
ggplot(flowers, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Iris Flower Measurements",
    subtitle = "Relationship between sepal length and petal length",
    x = "Sepal Length (cm)",
    y = "Petal Length (cm)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The colors form three visible groups. Setosa flowers have much shorter petals.
Virginica flowers generally have the longest petals and sepals. The upward
trend lines also show that flowers with longer sepals usually have longer
petals.

# Conclusion

In this tutorial, I used a built-in dataset to demonstrate a simple data
analysis process. I previewed the data, checked its structure, filtered rows,
selected columns, created a new variable, calculated group summaries, and made
a graph. These same steps can be used with many other datasets in R.
